title: Civil service reform
abstract: Civil service rules governing the selection and motivation of bureaucrats are among the defining institutions of modern democracies. Although this is an active area of reform in the US and elsewhere, economic analyses of the issue are virtually nonexistent. This paper provides a welfare evaluation of civil service reform. It describes the effect of reform on the interaction of politicians, voters, and bureaucrats, and shows that society often faces trade-offs between improving the bureaucracy and improving the performance of politicians. My results characterize the conditions under which merit-based recruitment and civil service protections such as tenure can improve welfare.
summary_en: Civil-service rules — merit-based recruitment, tenure protections, restrictions on political activity — are foundational to modern democracies, yet receive little economic analysis. Ujhelyi provides a formal welfare evaluation. Reform that strengthens civil service can improve bureaucratic performance but at a cost: it weakens the disciplining effect that politicians' control over bureaucrats can have on politician behaviour. The paper characterises conditions under which merit-based recruitment and tenure protections improve overall welfare versus when they don't, providing a clear analytical framework for civil-service reform debates.
data_used: Theoretical model — game-theoretic interaction between voters, politicians, and bureaucrats with reform parameters governing recruitment and tenure rules.
policy_relevance: Direct relevance for Hungarian public-administration reform. The 2010-onwards 'kormánytisztviselők' reorganisation, the 2018 special legal status of public service, and recurring debates about civil-service neutrality versus political accountability all map onto the paper's trade-offs. Useful framework for the Belügyminisztérium and the Public Service Commission when designing reform packages.
